Stick Broken Into Three Pieces (Cartesian)

ProbabilityCoordinatesParadoxes
Game: Break a stick in two places. Each pair of break points is a point in a square: find where the three pieces make a triangle, and how often that happens.
How to play: Drag the point P. Or choose an experiment and break sticks at random to see where the points land.

Look for the math

Break a stick of length 1 at two points, x and y, measured from its lower end. Each experiment is one point P = (x, y) of a unit square, in Cartesian coordinates. (The triangle version of this puzzle uses trilinear coordinates instead.)

The pink triangles

If x < y the pieces are x, y − x and 1 − y. The three triangle inequalities come down to

x < 1/2,   y − x < 1/2,   1 − y < 1/2

and the same with x and y swapped. Those points fill the two pink triangles, which join the centre of the square to the midpoints of two neighbouring sides. They cover 1/4 of the square. In the one-step experiment P is spread evenly over the square, so the chance of a triangle is 1/4.

Two steps: why not 1/3?

Break once at x, then break the longer piece. Points where the shorter piece was broken second (the green triangles, another quarter) can no longer happen. Pink is 1/3 of the rest, so the answer looks like 1/3. But it is not: the second break is spread over a piece shorter than the stick, so P is no longer even. Break 1000 sticks and the dots crowd near the sides. When the first piece has length h < 1/2, the chance is h/(1−h), and averaging gives

2 ∫01/2 h/(1−h) dh = 2 ln 2 − 1 ≈ 0.386

Asimov's thorn

Daniel Asimov always breaks the left piece again, at a fraction y of its length. Then the pieces are xy, x(1−y) and 1−x, and (x, y) is uniform in the square. The triangle region is a thorn between the line x = 1/2 and the hyperbolas xy = 1/2 and x(1−y) = 1/2, with area ln 2 − 1/2 ≈ 0.193. The original page offers this as the answer to the two-step problem. But breaking the left piece means half the time breaking the shorter one, so it answers a different question: which piece is broken is left to chance. Breaking always the longer piece doubles it to 2 ln 2 − 1. The logic test measured the regions and both chances on a fine grid, and ran 100,000 experiments of each kind.

Choose the two steps experiment and break 1000 sticks a few times. Where do the dots crowd, and where are there none at all?

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
